Climate · Science · Event attribution

The clouds carried 10% more water. Japan got 20% more rain.

Scientists reran six of Japan’s record downpours without human-caused warming. The result was not a vague warning about the future: every event became weaker, and one threshold-area almost halved.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 23, 2026 at 18:20 JST · 10 min read
Safety first

This research explains past August–September events; it is not a current weather warning. For live hazards and evacuation information, use the Japan Meteorological Agency’s official portal and local-government instructions.

A storm cannot be placed in a laboratory twice. The Chiba rain of August 13 and 14 cannot be sent back through the atmosphere after removing 170 years of greenhouse-gas emissions. Yet a Japanese research team has done the next closest thing: it reconstructed six exceptional downpours in a high-resolution weather model, then ran their counterparts in a climate without the warming that has accumulated since industrialization.

The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology and the Meteorological Research Institute published the comparison on Friday. Across six events from August 13 to September 21, estimated rainfall was 15.7% to 22.9% greater in the warmed simulations. The team summarized the result as “around 20%.” That is the central finding—but the mechanism makes it more revealing.

6Level-5-equivalent heavy-rain cases analyzed
15.7–22.9%estimated rainfall amplification
1–2 kmmodel grid spacing

The atmosphere in the target regions was roughly 1.3°C to 1.6°C warmer because of global warming, the study estimated. Its water-vapor content was 9.5% to 11.4% higher—close to the familiar physical relationship in which saturation vapor capacity rises by about 7% per degree Celsius. If moisture were the whole story, rainfall might have risen by a similar percentage.

It did not. Rainfall increased by roughly twice the water-vapor increase. The extra moisture also released heat as it condensed, strengthening rising air inside storm clouds and helping the clouds intensify.

Six different storms, the same direction

The study did not select a single spectacular map. Researchers systematically extracted August and September events for which special warnings equivalent to Japan’s highest alert level—Level 5—were issued for heavy rain, landslides or flooding. That produced six cases: Chiba; Ishikawa and Toyama; Fukui; Tokai; a widespread five-day rain episode; and Typhoon No. 25 from the northern Izu Islands into southern Kanto.

The smallest modeled increase, 15.7%, came during nine hours of Tokai rain on September 8. Fukui’s 24-hour event was the largest at 22.9%. Chiba and Typhoon No. 25 each reached 22.8%; the Ishikawa–Toyama event reached 18.6%; and the five-day widespread episode reached 20.8%. Different weather setups therefore produced different numbers, but no case reversed sign.

This is event attribution, a field designed to answer a narrower question than “Did climate change cause the storm?” Weather systems still need immediate triggers: a typhoon track, a front, unstable air, topography and timing. Attribution asks how a changed background climate altered the probability or intensity of the event that emerged from those ingredients.

The 300-millimeter threshold

Typhoon No. 25 gives the sharpest picture. It passed south of Kanto on September 20–21, producing record rain from the northern Izu Islands through Chiba and Kanagawa. Oshima Town received a Level 5 landslide special warning. Some observation points in Chiba set new 24- and 48-hour rainfall records.

Researchers simulated the 36 hours from noon September 20 through midnight September 21. Averaged over the defined region, warming increased modeled rainfall by 22.8%. At the Sakura AMeDAS station, observed 36-hour rain reached 352.5 millimeters—about 13.9 inches.

But the most consequential number concerns area, not a single gauge. In the counterfactual no-warming simulation, 1,400 one-square-kilometer grid cells crossed 300 millimeters. In the warmed reconstruction, 2,560 cells crossed it. The modeled footprint above that extreme threshold was about 1.8 times as large.

352.5 mmobserved 36-hour rain at Sakura
1,400grid cells above 300 mm without warming
2,560grid cells above 300 mm with warming

That is why “20% more rain” should not be pictured as a uniform extra layer spread across a map. Flooding and slope failure depend on thresholds, duration, drainage, soil and what has already fallen. A modest percentage change in an average can move a much larger area into a dangerous category.

How the team built a world that did not happen

The calculation used d4PDF, Japan’s large ensemble climate database. It contains past-climate runs, counterfactual runs that remove human-caused warming, and future experiments. For this analysis, researchers derived the warming difference from simulations corresponding to 2016–2025 and removed changes in air and sea-surface temperature from the event setup.

They then used high-resolution weather models: one-kilometer grids for the individual events and two-kilometer grids for the broad case. For the typhoon analysis, nine different initialization times, spaced three hours apart, were averaged to reduce sensitivity to a single model start.

This design does not mean the output is an exact measurement of an alternate Earth. Models simplify physics, event boundaries affect averages, and typhoon track or storm-cell placement can shift. The release uses careful language: the findings indicate a high possibility that warming increased the rainfall. It also says further work is under way on changes in rainfall distribution and typhoon intensity.

A second method points the same way

The release compares its quantitative simulations with work by Japan’s Weather Attribution Center, a researcher-led group established in May 2025. That team uses a “weather-map analogue” approach: machine learning searches large warmed and counterfactual ensembles for roughly 100 cases with pressure patterns resembling the real event, including how the pattern evolved.

The analogue studies found that warming raised heavy-rain risk in Chiba, Fukui and Kagoshima. Ishikawa–Toyama and Aichi–Gifu leaned in the same direction but needed more verification. Agreement between two different methods does not erase their uncertainties; it makes the shared direction harder to dismiss as an artifact of one technique.

Why a retrospective result matters now

The release arrived weeks after the water fell. That timing is a strength, not a failure of forecasting. Emergency forecasts tell people what to do before and during a storm. Attribution studies return afterward to ask what part of the damage environment has changed—and therefore what engineers, insurers and local governments should assume before the next storm.

A drainage standard based on yesterday’s rain distribution can become outdated even when the pipes have not changed. Hazard maps, evacuation routes, reservoir operation and slope protection face the same problem. The study does not prescribe a policy, but it quantifies the moving baseline beneath those choices.

For an overseas reader, Japan’s language of five alert levels can obscure the human decision. Level 5 is not the moment to begin evacuation; it means a life-threatening situation may already exist. Official guidance urges people to act by Level 4. The six analyzed cases entered the dataset because the weather was already at that highest end of the warning system.

The Japanese term for today is ōame—大雨, “heavy rain.” 大 means large; 雨 means rain. It appears in forecasts, warning names and phone alerts, not just conversation. Learning the characters can help a visitor recognize urgency, but language learning never replaces following local instructions.

The most important result is therefore not that climate change “made” six storms. It is that the same real-world circulation, placed over today’s warmer Japan, repeatedly produced more rain than its no-warming counterpart. In one typhoon, the model’s most extreme rainfall footprint expanded by 83%. The atmosphere did not merely hold more water. It turned that water into a larger hazard.
